extracted.intended_audience: employers, employee and employer advocates, labor lawyers, HR professionals, and other stakeholders affected by FLSA EAP exemption rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards the Department of Labor used to select and assess a new standard salary level for the EAP (white-collar) exemption, including data choices, objectives (duties primacy, screening function), impact analysis, and implementation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nonhourly worker earnings as proxy for salaried compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is continuing to use data on nonhourly worker earnings as a proxy for compensation paid to salaried workers because commenters did not provide any statistically robust data source that more closely reflects salary as defined in the Department's regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some commenters challenged this approach, the Department is not aware of, and commenters did not provide, any statistically robust data source that more closely reflects salary. The Department also believes relatively few nonhourly workers were paid by methods other than salaried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restricting dataset to exempt employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not limit the data set to employees already classified as exempt because doing so 'requires uncertain assumptions regarding which employees are actually exempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting the dataset to exempt employees introduces uncertainty about exemption status and undermines the analysis; the Department preferred broader datasets to avoid that methodological uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve primacy of the duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a salary-level methodology that preserves the primary role that an analysis of employee duties plays in determining EAP exemption status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One objective of the salary-level selection was to ensure that, for a significant majority of white-collar workers, duties — not salary — remain determinative of exemption status. The Department analyzed the distribution of earnings and probability of meeting duties to confirm duties primacy (e.g., 72% earn above the new level and have duties determinative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore salary level's initial screening function
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the salary level so that it fully restores the salary level's historical role as an initial screen that excludes lower-paid workers (particularly those below the long test salary level) from the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully restoring the screening function requires a salary level that ensures all employees who earn below the long test level are excluded from the exemption; the Department used the long test level as a key parameter in assessing appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for shift from two-test to one-test system
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a methodology that more effectively identifies bona fide EAP employees in a one-test system and reasonably distributes the impact of the shift between employees earning between the long and short test salary levels and their employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology must account for the removal of the long/short test structure and avoid outcomes that would inappropriately alter how many employees' exemption status is salary-determinative vs duties-determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set standard salary level at 35th percentile in lowest‑wage Census Region
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department sought to set the standard salary level at the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice was presented as meeting the three articulated objectives (duties primacy, restore screening function, and reasonable distribution of impact) and, based on the most recent data, produced $1,128 per week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the salary level determinative for too many employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid methodologies that would make the salary level determinative of exemption status for an excessive share of employees (a risk cited for the 2016 methodology set at the 40th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the 2016 methodology to current data would make salary determinative for 55% of employees between the long and short tests (vs. 40% under the Department's methodology). The Department expressed concern courts could find such an outcome problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid setting salary equal to short-test or excessively high percentiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set the salary level equivalent to the short test level or at a higher percentile (e.g., 55th) that would foreclose employers from exempting employees who historically were exempt and/or make salary unduly determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting salary at short-test levels would prevent employers from using the exemption for the population earning between long and short tests (historically exempt under the long test). Higher percentiles amplify the concern that salary eclipses duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place salary level below midpoint between long and short test levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a salary level that is below the midpoint between long and short test salary levels to balance excluding employees who perform substantial nonexempt work and enabling employers to exempt those who do not perform substantial nonexempt work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's final methodology produced a salary level lower than the midpoint, aiming to 'appropriately balance' screening for nonexempt work with employer flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical context but adjust for system differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider historical norms (e.g., percentiles in prior years) when evaluating salary-level appropriateness, but account for differences between the past two-test system and the current one-test system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons to 1975 short-test percentages are useful, but historical figures must be interpreted in light of the two-test system where a long test allowed some lower-paid workers to remain exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze impact across the universe of full-time salaried white-collar workers
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing salary-level impact, analyze effects on all full-time salaried white-collar workers (the universe of workers who could be impacted), not only currently exempt workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department examined distribution of earnings and estimated numbers above/below the proposed level (e.g., 45.4 million total, 12.7 million below new level), to put the salary level in context and confirm duties remain primary for most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probability codes to estimate who meets the duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ probability estimates (probability codes) to estimate the share of workers who meet the standard duties test when a direct measure is not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department has used these codes across multiple EAP rules, mapped occupational codes to current datasets using crosswalks, and validated appropriateness via O*NET review. It defended the continued reliability of the probability codes despite their age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map occupational codes and verify with O*NET / CPS MORG
rubrics_metrics.description: Use occupational crosswalks to map original probability-code occupations to 2018 Census occupational codes and verify with O*NET; use CPS MORG data for earnings distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department mapped codes to the 2018 Census occupational codes used in CPS MORG and reviewed O*NET to confirm probability codes reflected current occupational duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and decompose number of affected workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify the number of workers affected by salary-level changes and decompose impacts (initial update vs application of new standard salary level; effects relative to long/short tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., the Department estimated 4.0 million affected workers from standard salary level changes (1.0 million from initial update and 3.0 million from applying the new standard), and attributed 2.2 million of those to the increase from the long test to the new methodology while 1.8 million were due to restoring the historic screening function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for commenters' estimates and critiques but weigh validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider commenter-provided impact estimates and critiques (e.g., employer groups asserting higher affected-worker numbers), but evaluate their methodology and substantive challenges to the Department's analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters claimed much larger affected populations (Oxford Economics, AFPI), and some challenged probability codes; the Department compared and explained why it relied on its own validated estimates and why many commenters did not directly rebut key aspects of the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exempt nonprofit organizations from the salary-level test
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline requests to create special salary-level rules for nonprofits; employees of nonprofits remain subject to the same salary level, salary basis, and duties tests as other employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with historical practice, the Department declined special nonprofit exemptions but accounted for nonprofit concerns by setting the salary using the lowest-wage Census Region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline creation of enforcement carve-outs analogous to 2016 for Medicaid HCBS providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt a policy exempting certain Medicaid-funded service providers (e.g., small residential providers) from enforcement as was done related to the 2016 regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cited a smaller initial update and an approximately eight-month compliance timeframe, and committed instead to providing technical assistance and coordinating with CMS/ACL for impacted Medicaid-funded providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prorate the salary level for part-time employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject requests to prorate the salary level for part-time positions; the Department has never prorated and declines to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: part-time employees generally do not work >40 hours; overtime pay is typically not at issue. Employers may pay a nonexempt employee a salary for part-time work provided the salary equals at least the minimum wage when divided by the actual hours worked (<=40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain salary-basis example ratios; update only dollar amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When updating example figures in the salary-basis regulation (§541.604(b)), update the dollar amounts to reflect the new salary level but preserve the same ratios between actual and guaranteed earnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department updated numbers to account for the salary-level change but declined suggestions to alter the ratios in the example, which would have been a substantive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continue current rule on nondiscretionary bonuses counting toward salary (10% cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not increase the percentage of the salary level that may be satisfied by nondiscretionary bonuses and incentive payments; employers can continue to satisfy up to 10 percent of the salary level through such payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the final rule employers can satisfy up to 10 percent of the new salary level ($112.80 per week under this final rule) via nondiscretionary bonuses and incentive payments (including commissions) paid annually or more frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh potential employer harms but avoid speculative macroeconomic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider asserted negative effects (reclassification, loss of flexible/remote work, morale, reduced benefits, salary compression, price inflation), but do not let speculative or disputed macroeconomic impacts override statutory objectives and validated analytical findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reviewed employer concerns and employee counter-comments; found the macroeconomic implications speculative and in dispute, and determined they did not justify deviating from the proposed methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasonable implementation timeline and technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow an implementation period (e.g., approximately 8 months for certain providers) and commit to issuing technical assistance and coordinating with relevant agencies to support compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than adopt exemptions, the Department will offer technical assistance and coordinate with ACL and CMS for Medicaid-funded service providers impacted by the rule.
